statement: Five beads of five different colours are threaded on a circular bracelet. Two bracelets count as the same if one can be turned or flipped into the other. How many different bracelets are there?

choices.misconception: I divided the 120 arrangements by 6 rather than by the 10 movements that leave a bracelet looking the same.
I allowed for turning the bracelet but forgot it can also be flipped over.
I halved the 120 for flipping but forgot that turning also gives the same bracelet.
I counted every arrangement in a line, as if the bracelet had a fixed first bead.

hints: Count the arrangements, then count the repeats.

Start from all the arrangements as if the positions were fixed. Then work out how many of those are really the same bracelet: each one appears once per turn and again for each turn of the flipped version.
There are 120 arrangements. Each bracelet appears 5 times from turning and twice over from flipping, so 10 times in all: 120 divided by 10 = 12.

solutions.reliable: Overcount deliberately, then correct. Five distinct beads in five fixed positions give 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120 arrangements. But turning the bracelet by one, two, three or four positions gives the same bracelet, and so does flipping it over and turning it. That is 5 turns times 2 for the flip = 10 arrangements per genuine bracelet. So 120 divided by 10 = 12. The transferable idea: name exactly how many times each object was counted before dividing.
solutions.elegant: Hold one bead fixed to kill the turning, leaving 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 arrangements of the rest, then halve for the flip: 12.

whyOnTest: Deliberate overcounting followed by an exact correction is a genuine 5-point idea, and guessing the correction factor is what separates a right answer from a plausible one.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
